items.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals
items.summary:
A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979

Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio.

Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer.

items.t: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals

items.title: ‘It’s stressful but better than having a proper job’: the life of a cricket umpire

Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee

By Wisden Cricket Monthly

Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart.

More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare?

items.title: Rayan Cherki magic denies Napoli but Manchester City’s struggles continue
items.summary:
For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne.

Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat.

Continue reading...
items.t: Rayan Cherki magic denies Napoli but Manchester City’s struggles continue

items.title: Dortmund’s Beier halts Arsenal charge after thunderbolt from Gyökeres
items.summary:
Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday, this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres.

But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight.

Continue reading...

items.title: Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov
items.summary:
• Opening game ends in draw by repetition

  • Defending champion plays white in Game 2

  • Read our move-by-move report of Game 1

  • Sindarov: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’

Indian chess star Gukesh Dommaraju held off Javokhir Sindarov amid a mounting time crisis on Tuesday, drawing the opening game of their eagerly awaited $2.5m world title match in 38 moves at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the picturesque Geneva suburb of Cologny.

After spending more than 36 minutes on a single move and much of the afternoon racing against the clock, the defending champion said the time he invested early helped him play faster as a drawish position sharpened and his minutes dwindled opposite the in-form Uzbek challenger. “When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves,” Gukesh said. “And then the moves after that were pretty easy.”

French Football Federation president faces uphill battle to win backing of Africa’s decision-makers in Fifa election

Philippe Diallo must be learning very quickly that the battle to wrest the Fifa presidency from Gianni Infantino will be very challenging.

When Patrice Motsepe, the president of the Confederation of African Football (Caf), asked the presidents and general secretaries of its 54 member associations to give Infantino a standing ovation at Caf’s general assembly last weekend, Diallo, a guest at the event, had no choice but to cope with an uncomfortable moment.

items.title: Game over? How playing Grand Theft Auto VI is affecting elite athletes’ performances | Sean Ingle
items.summary:
Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad

“They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was ESPN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI.

Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “historique” after midnight on Thursday. Meanwhile before last weekend’s Premier League games, the Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would all lose. Why? Because their younger squads might be more focused on Vice City than their opponents, and therefore play with less intensity as a result. By Monday that forecast had been liked tens of thousands of times.
